reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant deficiency of coproporphyrinogen oxidase, the sixth enzyme of haem biosynthesis, one of the three hepatic acute porphyrias
Presents predominantly with acute neurovisceral attacks similar to acute intermittent porphyria, and less commonly with photocutaneous skin fragility, so it is also a mixed porphyria
Skin blistering, when present, resembles porphyria cutanea tarda but is generally milder and less frequent than in variegate porphyria
The biochemical hallmark is a marked, isolated increase in faecal and urinary coproporphyrin (predominantly the isomer III), with raised urinary ALA and PBG during attacks
Acute attacks are precipitated by the same factors as other acute porphyrias: porphyrinogenic drugs, fasting, alcohol, infection and hormonal changes
A rare biallelic (harderoporphyria) variant presents in the neonatal period with haemolytic anaemia and marked faecal harderoporphyrin excretion
Acute attacks are managed with trigger removal, carbohydrate/glucose loading and intravenous haem, as for other acute porphyrias
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary coproporphyria is caused by partial deficiency of coproporphyrinogen oxidase, the sixth enzyme of haem biosynthesis, which converts coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX. The block leads to accumulation and excretion of coproporphyrin III and, during metabolic demand, back-up of the neurotoxic precursors ALA and PBG through induction of hepatic ALA synthase. The neurotoxic precursors drive acute neurovisceral attacks, while occasional accumulation of photoreactive coproporphyrin in the skin produces a blistering photosensitivity. Homozygous or compound heterozygous defects affecting a specific enzyme step cause the more severe harderoporphyria phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Acute intermittent porphyria and variegate porphyria
Surgical acute abdomen during an attack
Porphyria cutanea tarda when skin blistering predominates
Guillain-Barre syndrome for the acute neuropathy
Secondary coproporphyrinuria from liver disease or other systemic illness
additionalInvestigations: Faecal porphyrin analysis showing predominant coproporphyrin III
Urinary ALA, PBG and coproporphyrin during symptomatic episodes
Plasma fluorescence scanning to help distinguish from variegate porphyria
Molecular genetic testing of the CPOX gene for confirmation and family screening
Serum sodium and renal function during attacks
Nerve conduction studies where motor neuropathy is suspected
redFlags: Progressive motor weakness or respiratory failure during an attack
Neonatal haemolytic anaemia suggesting the harderoporphyria variant
Administration of a porphyrinogenic drug in a symptomatic patient
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good with trigger avoidance and prompt treatment of attacks; cutaneous involvement is usually mild, though severe neurovisceral attacks carry risks comparable to other acute porphyrias.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish it biochemically from variegate porphyria, which alters counselling
Prescribing porphyrinogenic drugs that trigger attacks
Attributing isolated coproporphyrinuria to porphyria when it is secondary to liver disease or other illness
Missing the rare severe neonatal harderoporphyria presentation
Overlooking the diagnosis between attacks when biochemistry can normalise
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
